scope_note: Authoritative family-recognition backfill for the Hays/Central Texas learner. Platanaceae is monogeneric in current POWO, and the project pool contains one local anchor: Platanus occidentalis.

actions: Restored Proteales / Platanaceae to Platanus occidentalis in the Master Plant Pool.
Confirmed Platanus was already present in the hidden genus-family map.
Added a taxonomy/teaching note to the source row emphasizing the bud-in-petiole and fruit-head characters.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Start with the huge deciduous tree, mottled exfoliating bark and alternate palmately lobed leaves. Then inspect the twig: the swollen petiole base covers the axillary bud while the leaf is attached, and the stipule leaves an encircling scar. Reproductive confirmation comes from separate spherical male/female flower heads and persistent spherical fruiting heads packed with many achenes.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Exfoliating patchwork bark + alternate palmately lobed stipulate leaves + petiole base enclosing the axillary bud + annular stipule scar + pendulous globose heads of unisexual flowers/fruits.
core_characters: Deciduous trees; Platanaceae is monogeneric in current POWO.
Leaves alternate, simple, palmately lobed and coarsely toothed.
Young leaves and axes often carry branched/dendritic hairs.
Leaf-like stipules partly sheath the twig and leave a ring-like/encircling stipular scar.
Petiole base is enlarged and hollow, enclosing the axillary bud until leaf fall.
No true terminal bud; twigs can appear zigzag/knobby.
Flowers unisexual and the tree monoecious.
Male and female flowers are packed into separate dense spherical heads on long stalks.
Female flowers have a superior ovary with free carpels.
The mature spherical fruiting head is packed with many achenes/nutlets accompanied by long basal hairs that aid wind dispersal.
Bark exfoliates irregularly in plates, exposing pale chalky white, cream, tan, greenish or gray patches.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not identify Platanaceae from mottled bark alone; young trunks and lower bark can remain darker and scaly.
Do not confuse the spherical fruiting head with one single fruit; it is a head containing many individual achenes.
Do not teach sycamore leaves as opposite like maples; Platanus leaves are alternate.
Do not teach every spherical head as a fruit: male and female flowers also occur in separate spherical heads.
Do not use leaf lobing alone against Liquidambar or Acer; use bud/petiole, stipule scar, bark and fruit architecture.

anchor_card.status: Priority 1; Hays Local + NPSOT + Personal List; species-level curation still pending
anchor_card.taxonomy: Current POWO and FNA accepted species; native in Texas.
anchor_card.look_here_first: Bark first, then twig architecture: patchy white/tan/gray exfoliating upper trunk, huge alternate 3–5-lobed leaf, ring-like stipule scar, and the lateral bud hidden under the swollen petiole base.
confirms: Mottled exfoliating bark, especially conspicuous on upper trunk and major limbs.
Leaf-like stipules partly sheathing the twig.
Encircling stipule scar on the twig.
Petiole base swollen/hollow and covering the axillary bud while leaf is attached.
Monoecious, with separate male and female spherical flower heads.
Usually one mature fruiting ball per long stalk, occasionally two.
Fruiting head roughly 2.5–3 cm across in FNA.
Each head contains numerous 7–10 mm achenes with long basal hairs.
anchor_card.habitat: Frequently associated with alluvial soils, stream/lake margins, moist ravines and riparian settings; can also occur on limestone and uplands.

hidden_bud_lesson.key_point: One of the coolest sycamore twig characters is that the axillary bud is literally hidden by the swollen petiole base until the leaf falls.
hidden_bud_lesson.field_value: This works when there are no flowers or fruits and helps separate sycamore from superficially maple-like leaves.

stipule_lesson.key_point: Platanus has conspicuous leaf-like stipules that partly sheath the twig and leave an annular/encircling scar.
stipule_lesson.comparison: Maples lack this characteristic ring-like stipular scar/bud-in-petiole combination.

reproductive_lesson.monoecy: Male and female flowers occur on the same tree but in separate spherical heads.
reproductive_lesson.male_head: Small globose staminate head; breaks apart after pollen shed.
reproductive_lesson.female_head: Globose pistillate head with many tightly packed flowers/carpels.
reproductive_lesson.fruiting_head: Persistent brown fuzzy sphere containing numerous individual achenes with basal hairs.
reproductive_lesson.teaching_rule: Label the whole sphere as a fruiting head/infructescence and then zoom in to one achene.

fast_key: Huge deciduous tree + mottled exfoliating white/tan/gray bark -> check Platanus.
Alternate giant palmate leaf + swollen petiole base covering lateral bud -> Platanus strongly supported.
Ring-like stipule scar around twig + no true terminal bud -> Platanus twig confirmation.
Long-stalked fuzzy brown sphere that breaks into hairy achenes -> Platanus fruiting head.
Opposite palmate leaves + paired samaras -> Acer, not Platanus.
Alternate star-shaped leaves + woody spiny capsule ball -> Liquidambar, not Platanus.

Acer / Sapindaceae.confusion: Large palmately lobed leaves can look maple-like.
Acer / Sapindaceae.tie_breaker: Acer has opposite leaves and paired samaras. Platanus has alternate leaves, hidden bud under the petiole base, ring-like stipule scars, exfoliating bark and spherical achene heads.

Liquidambar.confusion: Alternate palmately lobed leaves and hanging spherical structures can look superficially similar.
Liquidambar.tie_breaker: Liquidambar leaves are more star-like and its persistent fruit ball is woody and spiny, made of capsules. Platanus fruit heads are fuzzy and disintegrate into many hairy achenes; Platanus also has the bud-enclosed-by-petiole character.
